title: FDA Approves First mRNA Flu Vaccine From Moderna for Adults Over 50
excerpt: The approval of mFlusiva marks a milestone for mRNA technology beyond COVID-19, giving older Americans a flu shot that was 27% more effective than standard vaccines in clinical trials.
body:
• The FDA approved Moderna's mFlusiva, the first mRNA-based seasonal flu vaccine, for adults aged 50 and older
  • The vaccine was 26.6% more effective than standard-dose flu shots in a late-stage trial of more than 40,000 adults
  • Moderna received traditional approval for ages 50–64 and accelerated approval for those 65 and older, with a post-marketing study required for the latter group
  • The mRNA platform allows faster strain updates — two to three months from selection to rollout versus six months for traditional egg-based vaccines

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Moderna's mFlusiva for adults aged 50 and older, the company announced Wednesday, making it the first mRNA-based vaccine licensed for seasonal influenza in the United States.

The approval follows a dramatic regulatory journey. The FDA initially rejected Moderna's application in February, citing concerns about trial design, before reversing course two weeks later and agreeing to review the shot. An advisory panel voted 9-0 in June that the vaccine's benefits outweigh its risks.

What the Data Shows

The approval rests on a late-stage trial enrolling more than 40,000 adults aged 50 and older during the 2024–25 flu season. The vaccine proved 26.6% more effective than a licensed standard-dose flu shot — a meaningful margin in a field where incremental gains are hard-won.

Moderna also submitted separate data showing mFlusiva generated stronger antibody responses than Sanofi's high-dose flu vaccine, Fluzone HD, in adults 65 and older. The FDA granted traditional approval for the 50–64 age group and accelerated approval for those 65 and above, requiring an additional confirmatory study for the older cohort.

Side effects were consistent with existing flu vaccines: injection-site pain, fatigue, headache, muscle and joint pain, and occasional fever.

Why mRNA Matters for Flu

Traditional flu vaccines rely on egg-based manufacturing, a decades-old process that requires strain selection roughly six months before distribution. This long lead time means the final product sometimes misses the mark on circulating strains.

Moderna's mRNA platform can compress that timeline to two to three months, potentially allowing manufacturers to make later strain selections that better match what's actually circulating when flu season arrives.

"Flu remains a significant public health challenge, and mFLUSIVA provides an important new option for America's seniors."

— Stéphane Bancel, CEO, Moderna

The World Health Organization recommended updating all three viral strains in 2026 flu vaccines due to a new A(H3N2) variant, underscoring the value of faster production cycles.

Market Implications

MFlusiva will compete with established flu vaccines from Sanofi, GSK, CSL Seqirus, and AstraZeneca. Analysts do not expect meaningful revenue until the second half of 2027, as Moderna missed the contracting cycle for the current U.S. flu season.

Still, the approval validates Moderna's post-pandemic strategy. The company has been counting on flu and a future COVID-flu combination shot to replace declining COVID vaccine revenue and prove the commercial durability of its mRNA platform. A combined mRNA vaccine targeting both COVID and influenza was approved in Europe earlier this year.

Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, told Healio he expects the vaccine to be available by September. Jefferies analyst Andrew Tsai has forecast $750 million in combined U.S. sales of Moderna's flu and combination vaccines by 2030.

The Diaspora Angle

For Indian Americans, who make up one of the fastest-growing demographics among U.S. seniors, the approval adds another option during flu season. South Asian adults over 50 face elevated cardiovascular risks that can compound flu complications, making effective vaccination particularly relevant.

What's Next

Moderna's vaccine still needs a recommendation from the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices before it can be widely administered. The company says it expects to have mFlusiva available this fall. The larger question is whether the approval accelerates FDA's willingness to greenlight other mRNA-based vaccines — including Pfizer's own mRNA flu candidates still in development — after a period of regulatory uncertainty under former Commissioner Marty Makary.
